These INDUCED SURFACE CHARGES set up their own field OPPOSING the external one, so the net field inside is the difference of the two:
\(E = E_{0} - E_{induced} = \dfrac{E_{0}}{K}\)
which is smaller than \(E_{0}\) by the factor K.
(III) THE POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE FALLS WHEN THE PLATES ARE BROUGHT CLOSER. The capacitor is charged and isolated, so its charge Q is fixed, and the field between the plates, \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{Q}{A\varepsilon_{0}}\), depends only on that charge and the plate area, NOT on the separation. Hence
\(V = Ed\)
with E constant, so reducing d reduces V in direct proportion. Equivalently, \(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\) increases while Q stays fixed, so \(V = \dfrac{Q}{C}\) falls.
(ii) The potential energy of three point charges is the sum over the three PAIRS, and here every pair is separated by the same side a:
\(U = \dfrac{k}{a}\left[q_{1}q_{2} + q_{1}q_{3} + q_{2}q_{3}\right]\)
Substituting \(q_{1} = q\), \(q_{2} = -4q\) and \(q_{3} = 2q\):
\(q_{1}q_{2} = (q)(-4q) = -4q^{2}\)
\(q_{1}q_{3} = (q)(2q) = +2q^{2}\)
\(q_{2}q_{3} = (-4q)(2q) = -8q^{2}\)
Adding:
\(U = \dfrac{k}{a}\left[-4q^{2} + 2q^{2} - 8q^{2}\right] = -\dfrac{10kq^{2}}{a}\)
To DISSOCIATE the system means to separate the three charges to infinity, where the potential energy is zero. The work done is therefore the change in potential energy:
\(W = U_{final} - U_{initial} = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{10kq^{2}}{a}\right)\)
\(W = +\dfrac{10kq^{2}}{a} = \dfrac{10q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a}\)
The work is POSITIVE, which says the system is BOUND: an external agent must supply energy to pull the charges apart, because the attractions of the \(-4q\) for the other two outweigh the mutual repulsion of q and 2q.

rows.stem:
(i) Answer the following giving reason :

(I) The electron drift speed is estimated to be only a few mm/s for currents in the range of a few amperes. How, then, is the current established almost the instant a circuit is closed ?

(II) A low voltage supply from which one needs high currents must have very low internal resistance. Why ?

(III) The assertion that V = IR is a statement of Ohm's law is not true. Why ?

(ii) Two cells of emfs 12 V and 6 V are connected in parallel as shown in the figure. Their internal resistances are 1 \(\Omega\) and \(0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\) respectively. Calculate the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell between points A and B.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — for sub-part (ii): two branches drawn in parallel between terminals A and B, the upper branch carrying a cell labelled '12 V, 1 ohm' and the lower a cell labelled '6 V, 0.5 ohm'. The stem gives both emfs and both internal resistances, but the RELATIVE POLARITY of the two cells is carried only by the drawn cell symbols, and the equivalent emf depends on it. Page idx 30.
rows.solution:
(i) (I) WHY THE CURRENT APPEARS INSTANTLY. The drift speed is indeed only millimetres per second, so an individual electron would take hours to travel the length of a circuit. But the current does not wait for any electron to make that journey. When the circuit is closed, the ELECTRIC FIELD is established throughout the conductor almost instantaneously, at a speed close to that of light, and it sets ALL the electrons everywhere in the wire drifting at once, including those already beside the bulb. The current is therefore established essentially the instant the switch closes, though it does take a little while to settle to its steady value.
(II) WHY A HIGH-CURRENT SUPPLY NEEDS LOW INTERNAL RESISTANCE. The current a cell delivers is
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}\)
and the largest it can ever supply is obtained by making the external resistance as small as possible, \(R = 0\):
\(I_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\)
So the maximum current is set by the emf divided by the INTERNAL resistance alone. If the supply is of low voltage, then \(\varepsilon\) is small, and the only way to make \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\) large is to make r very small indeed.
(III) WHY V = IR IS NOT ITSELF OHM'S LAW. The equation \(V = IR\) is merely the DEFINITION of resistance: any conductor whatever has a ratio of voltage to current, and that ratio may be called R at each operating point. Ohm's LAW is the stronger, empirical assertion that this ratio is CONSTANT, independent of V, so that a plot of I against V is a straight line through the origin. Many conductors fail that test: a diode, a transistor, a gas discharge and a thermistor all have a \(\dfrac{V}{I}\) that varies with V. For them \(V = IR\) still defines an R at each point, but Ohm's law does not hold.
(ii) For two cells in PARALLEL the equivalent emf is the weighted average of the two emfs, each weighted by the OTHER cell's internal resistance:
\(\varepsilon_{AB} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{1}r_{2} + \varepsilon_{2}r_{1}}{r_{1} + r_{2}}\)
Substituting \(\varepsilon_{1} = 12\) V with \(r_{1} = 1\ \Omega\), and \(\varepsilon_{2} = 6\) V with \(r_{2} = 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\):
\(\varepsilon_{AB} = \dfrac{12 \times 0{\cdot}5 + 6 \times 1}{1 + 0{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{6 + 6}{1{\cdot}5} = 8\ \mathrm{V}\)
The equivalent INTERNAL RESISTANCE is that of the two internal resistances in parallel:
\(r_{AB} = \dfrac{r_{1}r_{2}}{r_{1} + r_{2}} = \dfrac{1 \times 0{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{1}{3}\ \Omega \approx 0{\cdot}33\ \Omega\)
The equivalent cell has an emf of 8 V and an internal resistance of about \(0{\cdot}33\ \Omega\).
The emf is NOT the average of 12 and 6, which would be 9: the 6 V cell has the smaller internal resistance and therefore the greater weight, which drags the combined emf below the midpoint.
